The front of the church has a cylindrical cone spire. | static_image_caption = [[Bishop Auckland Town Hall]] }} '''Bishop Auckland''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɔː|k|.|l|ə|n|d}} {{respell|AWK|lənd}}) is a [[market town]] and [[civil parishes in England|civil parish]] at the confluence of the [[River Wear]] and the [[River Gaunless]] in [[County Durham]], England. It is {{convert|12|mi|km|0}} northwest of [[Darlington]] and {{convert|12|mi|km|0}} southwest of [[Durham, England|Durham]]. Much of the town's early history surrounds the [[Bishop of Durham|Bishops of Durham]] and the establishment of [[Auckland Castle]]'s predecessor, a hunting lodge, which became the main residence of Durham Bishops. This is reflected in the first part of the town's name.{{Harvnb |Simpson|1991|p=41}} During the [[Industrial Revolution]], the town grew rapidly as coal mining became its largest industry. Decline in the [[coal mining]] industry during the late twentieth century has changed the town's largest sector to manufacturing. Since 1 April 2009, the town's [[local authority]] has been [[Durham County Council]]. The [[unitary authority]] replaced the previous [[Wear Valley]] District and Durham County councils.{{citation | title = Make up of new unitary councils | work = BBC News | date = 1 April 2009 | url =https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/7976062.stm | access-date =6 June 2009}} The parliamentary constituency of [[Bishop Auckland (UK Parliament constituency)|Bishop Auckland]] is named after the town. It is currently held by [[Sam Rushworth]] of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]]. The town is twinned with the French town of [[Ivry-sur-Seine]]. ==History== ===Names=== The town was first attested under the name ''Alclit'' with ''Alcluith'' and ''Alcleat'' also found.{{Harvnb |Whellan|1856|p=274}}{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2009|p=5}} ''Auckland'' is an area name used in the settlements of [[St Helen Auckland]], [[West Auckland, County Durham|West Auckland]] and St Andrew Auckland, the latter an old name for [[South Church, County Durham|South Church]], all of which are along the path of the Gaunless.{{Harvnb |Simpson|2002|p=21}} The town was in the [[Bishop of Durham]]'s land, gaining the 'bishop' element to differentiate it from the other settlements.{{Citation|last= Gelling|first= Margaret|author2= W. F. H. Nicolaisen|author3=Melville Richards |title= The names of towns and cities in Britain|year=1970|publisher= Batsford|page= 53}} The name Gaunless is of [[Norsemen|Norse]] origin, thought to meaning ''useless''.{{Harvnb |Simpson|2002|p=132}} It is believed that this derives from the river's inability to power a mill, sustain fish or create fertile [[floodplains]].{{citation| last = Simpson | first = David | title = The North East England History Pages — Place Names | url = http://www.northeastengland.talktalk.net/Place%20Name%20Meanings%20A%20to%20D.htm | access-date = 26 August 2008 | archive-date = 13 September 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080913030434/http://www.northeastengland.talktalk.net/Place%20Name%20Meanings%20A%20to%20D.htm | url-status = dead }}{{citation | title = Echo Memories: Tides of change in the land of Canute | work = [[The Northern Echo]] | date = 20 July 2005 | url = http://www.northeasthistory.co.uk/the_north_east/history/echomemories/darlington/305/200705.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927173424/http://www.northeasthistory.co.uk/the_north_east/history/echomemories/darlington/305/200705.html | archive-date=27 September 2007 | access-date =26 August 2008 }} ====Auckland==== It is thought to be [[Cumbric language|Cumbric]], related to ''Alclud'' (which was the [[Kingdom of Strathclyde]]'s alternative name) meaning "cliff on the Clyde". It is thought 'Clyde' may be the [[river Gaunless]]'s ancient name.{{Citation |last=Ekwall |first=Eilert |title= The concise Oxford dictionary of place names |edition= 4 |year= 1960 |publisher=Oxford University Press |pages= 18–19}}{{cite journal|author=Bethany Fox|title='The P-Celtic Place-Names of North-East England and South-East Scotland'|journal=The Heroic Age|volume=10|date=2007|url=http://www.heroicage.org/issues/10/fox.html}} Historically attempts have been made to link Auckland to [[Old Norse]] ''Aukland'' meaning 'additional land'. This view of the name origin could refer to the area recorded as being extra land granted to the Bishop of Durham by [[King Canute]] in around 1020.{{Cite web|url=http://www.heroicage.org/issues/10/fox-appendix.html|title=Fox—P-Celtic Place-Names—Appendix|website=Heroicage.org|access-date=22 January 2022}} Another suggestion is that Auckland derives from Old English or Old Norse combination of 'oak' and 'land', a woodland in the area with a majority of oak trees with each settlement built between it and the river Gaunless. ===Early=== The earliest known reference to Bishop Auckland itself is around 1000 AD as land given to the Earl of Northumberland for defending the church against the Scots. It is also mentioned in 1020 as a gift given to the [[Bishop of Durham]] by [[King Canute]]. However, a village almost certainly existed on the town's present site long before this, with there being evidence of church on the site of St Andrew's Church in [[South Church, County Durham|South Church]] as early as the seventh century.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2009|p=4}} Furthermore, the [[Roman Empire|Romans]] had a look-out post where [[Auckland Castle]] is sited today and a {{convert|10|acre|km2|adj=on}} [[castra|fort]] at nearby [[Binchester]]. There is also evidence of possible [[Iron Age]] settlements around the town,{{PastScape | mnumber = 24313 | access-date =29 December 2008 }}{{PastScape | mnumber = 24335 | access-date =29 December 2008 }} together with finds of [[Bronze Age]],{{PastScape | mnumber = 24309 | access-date =29 December 2008 }} [[Neolithic]]{{PastScape | mnumber = 22197 | access-date =29 December 2008 }} and [[Mesolithic]]{{PastScape | mnumber = 24317 | access-date =29 December 2008 }}{{PastScape | mnumber = 23956 | access-date =29 December 2008 }} artefacts. === Bishops of Durham === [[File:Auckland Castle Crop.jpg|thumb|A portion of Auckland Castle]] Much of the town's history surrounds its links with the [[Bishops of Durham]]. In 1083, [[Prince bishop|Bishop]] [[William de St-Calais]] expelled a number of canons from [[Durham, England|Durham]]. Some of these settled in the area and established a [[collegiate church]]. Around 1183 Bishop [[Hugh Pudsey|Pudsey]] established a [[manor house]] in the town, with a great hall being completed in 1195 on the site occupied by St Peter's Chapel today.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=14}} Bishop [[Antony Bek (bishop of Durham)|Bek]], who preferred the town as his main residence over [[Durham Castle]] due to its proximity to hunting grounds, later converted the manor house into a castle. The grounds of the castle were noted as being large enough to contain 16,000 men ahead of the [[Battle of Neville's Cross]] in 1346. Between 1283 and 1310, Bek was also responsible for ordering the replacement of the collegiate church established in 1183 with the Church of St Andrew that stands in South Church today, together with accommodation for the canons; the building known today as the East Deanery.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2009|p=9}} The collegiate church also appears to have supported a school. The collegiate church was re-organised under Bishop [[Thomas Langley|Langley]] in 1428 and at some point in the same century moved to the castle grounds. The college and its school were finally dissolved in the 16th century.{{citation |last=Laurie |first=Barbara |title=A Short History of Bishop Auckland |publisher=Bishop Auckland Town |url=http://www.bishopauckland.org/history1.asp?HistoryId=15 |access-date=26 August 2008 |archive-date=25 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725080535/http://www.bishopauckland.org/history1.asp?HistoryId=15 |url-status=dead }}{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|p=543}}{{citation |first=William |last=Page |series=Victoria History of the Counties of England |title=A history of the County of Durham |volume=1 |year=1905 |publisher=Constable |pages=397–398}} The school was not revived until the reign of [[James I of England|King James I]] when in 1604 Anne Swifte petitioned the King to found a school and the Free Grammar School of King James, the direct antecedent of today's King James I school, was established. Although the school's early location is unknown, in 1638 Bishop [[Thomas Morton (bishop)|Morton]] granted the school space in an old chapel in the Market Place.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=75}} Also in 1604, James's son, the future King [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] made the first of three visits to the town. On this visit, his first to England, he was entertained by Bishop [[Tobias Matthew|Matthew]]. In 1617 James himself stayed in [[Auckland Castle]] between 17 and 19 April.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=15}} Later, on 8 May, at [[Durham Castle]] King James is reputed to have rebuked Bishop [[William James (bishop)|William James]] so badly that the Bishop returned to Auckland Castle and died three days later. Charles's second visit to the town was on his way to Scotland on 31 May 1633, when he was entertained by Bishop Morton. His third visit on 4 February 1647 was in less lavish circumstances, as a prisoner. Morton had fled the town in 1640 and the castle was empty.{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|p=547}} Consequently, the king had to stay in a [[public house]] off the Market Place owned by Christopher Dobson.{{citation |title=Castle State Rooms |publisher=[[Auckland Castle]] |url=http://www.auckland-castle.co.uk/downloads/aucklandcastlehistory.pdf |access-date=16 September 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110904163359/http://www.auckland-castle.co.uk/downloads/aucklandcastlehistory.pdf |archive-date=4 September 2011 }} [[File:NPG-Haselrig-Hesilrige.webp|thumb|upright|[[Arthur Haselrig|Sir Arthur Hazelrig]]|alt=A portrait of a man dressed in black armour. He has long brown hair down to his shoulders and a thin moustache and beard. His left hand is holding a helmet which is resting on a pedestal. His right hand is holding a small pole or scroll]] [[File:Auckland Castle - Chapel.jpg|thumb|St Peter's chapel. Originally the castle's great hall, it was converted to a chapel after the [[English Restoration|restoration]] of the monarchy.|alt=A two to three-storey high stone building. The building is topped with castellations and pinnacles]] After the disestablishment of the [[Church of England]], at the end of the [[First English Civil War|first civil war]], Auckland Castle was sold to [[Arthur Haselrig|Sir Arthur Hazelrig]], who demolished much of the castle, including the chapel, and built a mansion.{{Citation | last = Lightfoot | first = Joseph Barber | title = Leaders in the Northern Church: Sermons Preached in the Diocese of Durham | publisher = Macmillan | year = 1892 | page =140 }}{{Citation | last = Dodds | first = Glen Lyndon | title = Historic Sites of County Durham | publisher = Albion | year = 1996 | isbn = 978-0-9525122-5-7 | location = Sunderland | page = 16 }}{{Harvnb |Whellan|1856|p=279}} After the [[English Restoration|restoration]] of the monarchy, the new bishop of Durham, [[John Cosin]], in turn demolished Hazelrig's mansion and rebuilt the castle converting the banqueting hall into the chapel that stands today.{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|p=548}} === Industrial Revolution === By 1801, the town had a population of 1,861.{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|p=545}} At the end of the eighteenth century the town had no notable roads other than the Roman road, and little trade beyond weaving.{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|p=558}}{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|p=552}} Although, coal mining had existed on a small-scale as early as 1183 when it is mentioned in the [[Boldon Book]], it was limited by the lack of an easy way to transport coal away from the area.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=33}} All this changed with the arrival of railways in the early nineteenth century, which allowed large scale coal mining.{{Harvnb |Whellan|1856|p=276}} The railways allowed coal to be mined, and then transported to the coast before being put onto ships to London and even abroad.{{Harvnb |Whellan|1856|p=292}} [[File:Shute Barrington by Lawrence.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Shute Barrington]]|alt=A portrait of a large man dressed in a white gown.]] Around the same time, the bishop, [[Shute Barrington]] was a keen proponent of the use of education to improve the social and moral circumstances of the lower social classes. He used £70,000 received from lead mining royalties in Weardale to fund the establishment of a number of schools in the area. One of these schools was the Bishop Barrington School (now [[Bishop Barrington Academy]]), one of the town's three comprehensive schools today.{{Citation | last = Hunt | first = Christopher John | title = The lead miners of the Northern Pennines: in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries | location = Manchester | publisher = Manchester University Press | year = 1970 | page = [https://archive.org/details/leadminersofnort0000hunt/page/236 236] | isbn = 978-0-7190-0380-6 | url = https://archive.org/details/leadminersofnort0000hunt/page/236 }} The Bishop Barrington School opened on 26 May 1810, the Bishop's own birthday. The school even allowed girls to attend until the age of 11 years.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|pp=76–77}} Barrington's support of education for the poor was not without controversy. Some suggested education of the poor would lead people to question their position in society, others even blamed it for the [[French Revolution]].{{Cite ODNB | contribution = Barrington, Shute (1734–1826) | year = 2004 | title = Oxford Dictionary of National Biography | last = Varley | first = E. A. | doi = 10.1093/ref:odnb/1534 | url = http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/1534 | access-date =29 September 2009 }}{{Citation | last = Soloway | first = R. A. | title = Prelates and people: ecclesiastical social thought in England, 1783–1852 | location = London | publisher = Taylor & Francis | year = 1969 | page = [https://archive.org/details/prelatespeopleec0000solo/page/356 356] | isbn = 978-0-7100-6331-1 | url = https://archive.org/details/prelatespeopleec0000solo/page/356}} Barrington's successor, [[William van Mildert]] was involved in the creation of [[Durham University]]. [[Durham Castle]] was donated to the new university and Auckland Castle, usually the preferred residence by successive Bishops, became the Bishop of Durham's official residence in 1832. However, the influence of the bishops of Durham was on the wane and there was pressure for reform. Van Mildert would be the last ruler of the county palatine. Shortly after his death, in 1836, the position was stripped of its ancient powers and wealth.{{Cite ODNB | contribution = Mildert, William Van (1765–1836) | year = 2004 | title = Oxford Dictionary of National Biography | last = Varley | first = E. A. | doi = 10.1093/ref:odnb/28096 | url = http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/28096 | access-date =29 September 2009 }}{{Citation| last = Brickstock | first = Richard | title = Durham Castle: Fortress, Palace, College | location = Lindley | publisher = Jeremy Mills Publishing | year = 2007 | pages = 52–53 | isbn = 978-1-905217-24-3}} The population at the time of the 1841 census was 3,776 inhabitants.{{cite book |title=The National Cyclopaedia of Useful Knowledge |date=1848 |publisher=Charles Knight |location=London |page=638|volume=V |edition=First}} By 1851 the population of the town had increased to 5,112, with a great proportion of them working in ironworks and collieries. By 1891, the population had doubled again.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=56}} In the second half of the nineteenth century there were typically around 60 collieries in the area open at any one time.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=48}} By the turn of the twentieth century 16,000 people were employed in the mining industry in the area.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=43}} The town also became an important centre for rail, with large amounts of minerals such as coal, [[limestone]] and [[ironstone]] mined in the surrounding area passing through the town on the way to the coast.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=44}} In the neighbouring town of [[Shildon]] large numbers were employed in the railways, where a railway engine works was established.{{Harvnb|Fordyce|1857|pp=567–569}} ===Industrial decline=== By the early years of the twentieth century coal mining started to go into decline as coal reserves started to become exhausted. By the end of the 1920s unemployment had hit 27% and the population too had started to decline, as colliery employment had halved compared with ten years previously.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|pp=82–84}}{{Citation | last = Bulmer | first = Martin | title = Mining and Social Change: Durham County in the Twentieth Century | location = London | publisher = Taylor & Francis | year = 1978 | page = 145 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=kwIOAAAAQAAJ | isbn = 978-0-85664-509-9 | access-date =6 June 2009}} With the onset of the [[Great Depression]] unemployment rose to 60% in 1932 before easing back to 36% in 1937. The [[World War II|Second World War]] offered a temporary reprieve for the coal industry, however, after the war the decline continued.{{Citation |title = Thematic Overview — Industrial |publisher = Durham County Council |url = http://www.keystothepast.info/k2p/usp.nsf/pws/Keys+to+the+Past+-+Overviews+-+Industrial |access-date = 29 August 2008 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080828062239/http://www.keystothepast.info/k2p/usp.nsf/pws/Keys+to+the+Past+-+Overviews+-+Industrial |archive-date = 28 August 2008}} The last deep colliery in the area closed in 1968, although drift mines and the much more mechanised and less labour-intensive surface level opencast mining did continue.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=104}} Equally, the railways that had also supported the area were also scaled back, ultimately culminating in the closure of Shildon's Wagon works in 1984 with the loss of thousands of jobs.{{citation |title = Railway works resurrected decades after closure blow |publisher = [[The Northern Echo]] |date = 10 August 2006 |url = http://archive.thenorthernecho.co.uk/2006/8/10/226520.html |access-date = 26 August 2008 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120219131218/http://www.newsquest.co.uk/ |archive-date = 19 February 2012 |url-status = dead}} A 2016 report on the community stated that{{cite web|url=https://www.ilivehere.co.uk/statistics-bishop-auckland-durham-3726.html|title=Socio-Economic Statistics For Bishop Auckland, Durham|publisher=I Live Here|date=25 June 2016}}
the rate of unemployment in Bishop Auckland is both higher than the average for and higher than the national average{{nbsp}}... The rate of claiming any benefit (which includes in work benefits) is more than 25% higher in Bishop Auckland than the national average, suggesting that many people maybe under employed or on a low salary.
==Economy== At the end of the eighteenth century the town is noted as having little trade beyond weaving. The first mention of coal mining in the area is in the [[Boldon Book]] of 1183,{{Harvnb |Simpson|1991|p=25}} but early coal mining was limited by the lack of an easy way to transport coal away from the area. The arrival of the railways transformed the town as it allowed coal to be mined, and then transported to the coast before being put onto ships to London and even abroad. At the start of the twentieth century 16,000 people were employed in the mining industry in the area. However, by 1915 the coal industry in the town had started to decline as coal reserves started to become exhausted. The last deep colliery in the area closed in 1968. Today, with the decline of the Durham coalfield, manufacturing has been left as the largest sector of employment in the town, accounting for 24.6% of the town's employment. The town also traditionally had a strong retail sector.{{citation | title = £2.4 m 'people's plan' to revive economy of market town | work = [[The Northern Echo]] | date = 9 August 2000 | url = http://archive.thenorthernecho.co.uk/2000/8/9/194536.html | access-date =26 August 2008 }} As one of the county's main population centres with good bus and rail connections, and thriving markets on Thursdays and Saturdays, shoppers were attracted from smaller settlements on the Durham coalfield for miles around. However, the decline in the coal mining industry, along with increased car ownership and competition from local shopping malls such as the [[MetroCentre (shopping centre)|MetroCentre]] in A Durham County Councillor said that the funds would help the partners (including the Auckland Project) to regenerate the town center area for the benefit of all residents of the community.{{cite web|url=https://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/news/north-east-towns-land-175m-16878413 |title=North East towns land £175m from Government fund|date=6 September 2019 |publisher=Trinity Mirror North East|access-date=5 November 2019}} ===Building tourism in the town=== [[File:Auckland Castle 003.jpg|thumb|Auckland Castle gate and Market Place]] An October 2019 article in ''[[The Guardian]]'' referred to Bishop Auckland as a "rundown town ... since the closure of the mines" but predicted that the re-opening of Auckland Castle would transform the community into a "leading tourist destination". The castle re-opened on 2 November 2019 after renovations by the Auckland Project; the founding partner of the group is the owner of the castle, [[Jonathan Ruffer]] who purchased the property and all of the contents in 2012, including the artwork, which included the works by [[Francisco de Zurbarán]].{{cite web|url=https://www.aucklandproject.org/zurbaran-paintings/|title=Zurbarán Paintings|work=The Auckland Project|access-date=28 October 2019|archive-date=28 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728230018/https://www.aucklandproject.org/zurbaran-paintings/|url-status=dead}} [[File:St. Peter's Chapel at Auckland Castle - formerly the Banqueting Hall.jpg|thumb|St. Peter's Chapel at Auckland Castle, formerly the Banqueting Hall]] News reports in 2019 clarified the situation, stating that in 2012, Ruffer had purchased the castle and all of the contents, including the artwork, which included the works by Francisco de Zurbarán. The paintings which had been on tour, were returned to the site in time for the re-opening of the castle to visitors on 2 November 2019 as the Auckland Project,{{cite web|url=https://www.historichouses.org/houses/house-listing/auckland-castle.html|title=Auckland Castle MARKET PLACE, BISHOP AUCKLAND, CO DURHAM, DL14 7NR|publisher=The Auckland Project|access-date=28 October 2019|archive-date=20 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120142101/https://www.historichouses.org/houses/house-listing/auckland-castle.html|url-status=dead}} after a multi-million pound restoration project, funded partly by the National Lottery. By the time of the opening day, a new 35 meter high tower had been erected as a visitor centre; the structure has a lift and a staircase as well as balconies for views of the castle from above. The interior had been fully restored, including the bishops' "palatial" quarters. According to one news item, "each of the 14 restored rooms, recreated from contemporary accounts and personal recollections" features the career of one former bishop.{{cite web|url=https://www.theartnewspaper.com/news/castle-opening-crowns-gbp150m-revival-of-bishop-auckland |title=Castle opening crowns £150m revival of Bishop Auckland|date=November 2019 |publisher=The Art Newspaper|access-date=5 November 2019}} The Faith Museum of world religion and a huge glass greenhouse were under construction on Castle property.{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2019/nov/05/hothouse-towers-auckland-castles-skyscraping-pineapple-friendly-revamp |title=Hothouse towers: Auckland Castle's skyscraping revamp |date=5 November 2019 |work=The Guardian}} Other attractions already operating at or near the Castle include the Mining Art Gallery (in a nearby former bank building in the town centre) showing work mainly by self-taught or night school-educated miners; this attraction opened in 2017 (thanks to support provided to the Castle Trust by Bishop Auckland and Shildon AAP and Durham County Council);{{cite web|url=https://www.aucklandproject.org/news/mining-art-gallery-moving-ahead/|title=MINING ART GALLERY MOVING AHEAD|publisher=The Auckland Project|access-date=3 November 2019}} a 7.5 acre open-air theatre, [[Kynren]], on the other side of the River Wear, with a cast of 1,000 depicting the history of England;{{cite web|url=https://www.kynren.com/|title=Kynren|publisher=Eleven Arches|access-date=3 November 2019 |quote=Kynren brings to ground-shaking life the story of invasions, royal splendour, wars, heroic sacrifice, daily life and seismic change....Take your seat with 8,000 others}} and the Bishop Trevor Gallery at the Castle. The latter started displaying the [[National Gallery]]'s Masterpiece touring exhibit in October 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2019/nov/02/restored-auckland-castle-county-durham-bishop-auckland|title=First look: a tour of the restored Auckland Castle|work=The Guardian|date=2 November 2019 |access-date=3 November 2019}} In future, other attractions were expected to open in or near the town centre: * the Spanish Gallery opened in 2021. The display of Spanish "[[Spanish Golden Age|Golden Age]]" art occupies two converted buildings one of which housed [[Backhouse's Bank]]) * the Faith Museum opened in 2023. It is housed in the Scotland Wing of the castle and a purpose-built extension * a gallery that will feature medieval to later era artworks * a boutique hotel (in former pubs) and two restaurants in addition to the current bishop's Kitchen café. According to ''[[The Guardian]]'',
"The aim is to make the town – the heart of the abandoned Durham coalfields – a tourist destination that holds people for a day or two rather than just a couple of hours. The scheme will create hundreds of entry-level jobs in a county that suffers high unemployment and has some of the most deprived areas in northern Europe".
A ''[[Financial Times]]'' report in early November 2019 stated that "Kynren [theatre] has attracted 250,000 people and the Auckland Project, even with the castle closed, welcomed 35,500 visitors in the past year" to this community.{{cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/0101ffee-f5e7-11e9-9ef3-eca8fc8f2d65 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/https://www.ft.com/content/0101ffee-f5e7-11e9-9ef3-eca8fc8f2d65 |archive-date=10 December 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=City philanthropist battles to transform 'left behind' UK town|work=Financial Times|date=November 2019 |access-date=5 November 2019}} In 2025, ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' reported that Jonathan Ruffer had given at least £200 million to the Auckland Project.{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/destinations/europe/united-kingdom/bishop-auckland-jonathan-ruffer/ |title=A wealthy Christian spent £200m reviving this northern town – but not everyone is happy |last=Miles |first=Paul |website=The Telegraph |location=London |url-access=subscription |date=12 April 2025 |access-date=12 April 2025}} ==Governance== ===Historic=== {{further|County Palatine of Durham}} For a large part of the area's history, the autonomous powers held by the bishop of Durham meant that the county operated as a principality under England's [[protectorate]]. The UNESCO site describes the role of the bishops in the "buffer state between England and Scotland":{{cite web |url=https://www.durhamworldheritagesite.com/history/prince-bishops |title=The Prince Bishops of Durham |date=11 July 2011 |publisher=Durham World Heritage Site}}
From 1075, the Bishop of Durham became a Prince-Bishop, with the right to raise an army, mint his own coins, and levy taxes. As long as he remained loyal to the king of England, he could govern as a virtually autonomous ruler, reaping the revenue from his territory, but also remaining mindful of his role of protecting England's northern frontier.
A steward of Bishop [[Antony Bek (bishop of Durham)|Antony Bek]] in the thirteenth century is quoted as saying England had two kings; the king and the bishop of Durham.{{Harvnb |Simpson|1991|p=1}} A 1788 report states that the Bishops had the authority to appoint judges and barons and to offer pardons.{{cite book |last=Drummond Liddy |first=Christian |title=The Bishopric of Durham in the Late Middle Ages |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R6ZbDEhf86sC&q=durham+bishop+princes&pg=PA2 |publisher=Boydell |page=1 |isbn=978-1843833772|year=2008 }} The bishops of Durham were not stripped of the last of their secular powers until shortly after the death of Bishop [[William Van Mildert]] in 1836 by the [[Durham (County Palatine) Act 1836]].{{cite book |date=1836 |title=The Statutes of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eFk0AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA130 |publisher=His Majesty's Statute and Law Printers|page=130}} ===Modern=== At the end of the nineteenth century the [[Local Government Act 1894]] created Bishop Auckland [[Urban district (Great Britain and Ireland)|Urban District]] council. From 1894 to 1974, the town was governed by the Urban District council within the [[administrative county]] of [[County Durham|Durham]]. The district was enlarged to include a number of surrounding settlements in 1937 when Auckland [[Rural District]] and [[Willington, County Durham|Willington]] Urban District were abolished.{{Citation | title = A vision of Bishop Auckland UD | publisher =A vision of Britain | url = http://www.visionofbritain.org.uk/unit_page.jsp?u_id=10042847 | access-date =28 August 2008 }} The Urban District was replaced, under the [[Local Government Act 1972]], by a two tier district ([[Wear Valley]]) and county system. The former urban district area was re-parished from the May 2007 local elections with a new town council was established. After the elections, the council elected Barbara Laurie as the town's first re-established mayor.{{citation |title=New Town Council for Bishop Auckland |publisher=Wear Valley District Council |url=http://www.wearvalley.gov.uk/index.cfm?articleid=11791 |access-date=26 August 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927222613/http://www.wearvalley.gov.uk/index.cfm?articleid=11791 |archive-date=27 September 2007 }} On 25 July 2007, Durham County Council and Wear Valley District Council were replaced on 1 April 2009 by a single [[unitary authority]] serving the whole of County Durham.{{citation | title = Durham unitary authority approved | work = BBC News | date = 25 July 2007 | url = https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/wear/6915882.stm | access-date =26 August 2008 }} ===Parliament=== The town is a part of the [[Bishop Auckland (UK Parliament constituency)|Bishop Auckland parliamentary constituency]], and is currently represented at [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Westminster]] by [[Sam Rushworth]] MP ([[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]]). Prior to [[Brexit]], for the [[European Parliament]] its residents voted to elect [[Members of the European Parliament|MEP]]'s for the [[North East England (European Parliament constituency)|North East England]] constituency. ===Other=== The town is located in the South Area of the [[Durham Constabulary]],{{citation |title=South Area |publisher=[[Durham Constabulary]] |url=http://www.durham.police.uk/local/south/bishopauckland/ |access-date=12 January 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090309061804/http://www.durham.police.uk/local/south/bishopauckland |archive-date=9 March 2009 }} and served by the [[County Durham and Darlington Fire and Rescue Service]] and [[North East Ambulance Service]]. Bishop Auckland is twinned with the French town of [[Ivry-sur-Seine]], whilst the wider Wear Valley district was twinned with [[Bad Oeynhausen]] in Germany. {{Citation |title=Town Twinning |publisher=Wear Valley District Council |url=http://www.wearvalley.gov.uk/index.cfm?articleid=3913 |access-date=29 August 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204011407/http://www.wearvalley.gov.uk/index.cfm?articleid=3913 |archive-date=4 December 2008 }} === Town Hall === {{Main|Bishop Auckland Town Hall}} The Town Hall is a "Gothic style" [[Victorian architecture|Victorian]] Building overlooking the town's market place and is Grade II* listed.{{citation|title=Bishop Auckland Town Hall|url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1297550&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway|access-date=21 September 2009}} After being abandoned and then condemned for demolition in the 1980s, the town hall was fully restored in the early 1990s. It now houses the town's main [[public library]], a [[theatre]], an [[art gallery]], tourist information centre and a café-bar.{{Harvnb|Hutchinson|2005|pp=121–122}} The Town Hall has held three exhibitions for mining artist [[Tom Lamb (artist)|Tom Lamb]]. The first was held in 1999 for his 'Fading Memories' exhibition, then in 2004 for Lamb's 'The Footprints of My Years' exhibition and in 2008 the last exhibition called 'My Mining Days' was held. ==Geography== Bishop Auckland is located at {{Coord|54|39|36|N|1|40|48|W|type:city(24392)_region:GB-DUR}} ([[British national grid reference system]]: {{gbmapscaled|NZ208294|10|NZ208294}}) on the Durham coalfield at the confluence of the [[River Wear]] with its [[tributary]] the River Gaunless. The town nestles in the rivers' valley about {{convert|100|m|ft}} above [[sea level]]. Besides this the town is all but is surrounded on all sides by hills ranging in height from around {{convert|150|m|ft}} above sea level to over {{convert|220|m|ft}} above sea level. Bishop Auckland is located about {{convert|12|mi|km}} northwest of [[Darlington]] and {{convert|12|mi|km}} southwest of [[Durham, England|Durham]]. The town is served by [[Bishop Auckland railway station]], which marks the point where the [[Tees Valley Line]] becomes the [[Weardale Railway]]. The town is not served directly by any [[motorway]]s. Notable wards include Cockton Hill, Woodhouse Close, and Henknowle. Additionally, once neighbouring villages such as [[South Church, County Durham|South Church]], [[Tindale Crescent]], [[St Helen Auckland]], and [[West Auckland, Durham|West Auckland]] now more or less merge seamlessly into the town. == Demography == {| id="toc" style="float: right; margin-left: 2em; font-size: 90%;" cellspacing="5em" |- !colspan="4"| Bishop Auckland compared |- | '''[[United Kingdom Census 2001|UK Census 2001]] {{Citation | title = 2001 Census Profiles (Rates) for Major Centres in County Durham | publisher = Durham County Council | url = http://www.durham.gov.uk/PDFApproved/MCCatchmentSummarySheetsRates.pdf | access-date = 6 June 2009 }}{{dead link|date=July 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}{{Citation |title=2001 Census Profiles (Numbers) for Major Centres in County Durham |publisher=Durham County Council |url=http://www.durham.gov.uk/PDFApproved/MCCatchmentSummarySheets.pdf |access-date=29 August 2008 }}{{dead link|date=November 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}'''||'''Bishop Auckland'''||'''[[County Durham]]'''||'''England and Wales''' |- |Total population||24,392||493,484||52,041,916 |- |Foreign born||1.5%||2.0%||8.9% |- |Buddhist||0.2%||0.1%||0.3% |- |Christian||84.8%||83.5%||71.7% |- |Hindu||0.2%||0.1%||1.1% |- |Muslim||0.2%||0.2%||3.0% |- |No religion||7.3%||9.3%||14.8% |- |Over 65 years old||17.2%||16.7%||15.46% |- |Unemployed||5.0%||4.8%||4.3% |} According to the 2001 census, Bishop Auckland has a population of 24,392, living in 10,336 dwellings. Additionally [[Escomb Church|Escomb Saxon Church]],{{citation|title=The Saxon Church, Saxon Green, Escomb|url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1292122&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway|access-date=21 September 2009}} St Andrew's parish church,{{citation|title=Church of St Andrew|url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1196458&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway|access-date=21 September 2009}} St Helen's church,{{citation|title=Church of St Helen |url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1196602&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway |access-date=21 September 2009}} St Helen Hall,{{citation |title=St Helen Hall |url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1297566&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway |access-date=21 September 2009}} West Auckland Manor House,{{citation |title=The Manor House |url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1209970&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway |access-date=21 September 2009}} the East Deanery{{citation |title=East Deanery |url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1196576&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway |access-date=21 September 2009}} and the 14th century Bishop Skirlaw bridge are all Grade I listed.{{citation|title=Newton Cap Bridge|url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1292118&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway|access-date=21 September 2009}} Other notable buildings include the town hall, a Victorian railway viaduct and [[Vinovia|Binchester Roman fort]].{{cite web|url=http://www.durham.gov.uk/article/2011|title=Binchester Roman Fort – Durham County Council|publisher=Government of the United Kingdom}} === Auckland Castle === {{Main|Auckland Castle}} [[File:Auckland Castle - Gatehouse.jpg|thumb|[[Auckland Castle]]'s Gatehouse|alt=A crenellated stone arched gateway. In the middle is a small tower with a blue clock]] [[Auckland Castle]] (often known locally as ''The Bishop's palace''), was the official residence of the Bishop of Durham since 1832 until 2012. However, its history goes back much earlier, being established as a hunting lodge for the bishops of Durham.{{Citation |title=Castle History |publisher=[[Auckland Castle]] |url=http://www.auckland-castle.co.uk/castle-history.asp |access-date=25 August 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080928062749/http://www.auckland-castle.co.uk/castle-history.asp |archive-date=28 September 2008 }} The castle is surrounded by {{convert|800|acre|km2}} of parkland, which was originally used by the Bishops for hunting and is today open to the public.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=20}} The castle and its grounds contain seven Grade I listed structures.{{citation |title=Auckland Castle |url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1196444&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway |access-date=21 September 2009}}

The site also includes three new restaurants for visitors, with one in operation by early November 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2019/oct/25/auckland-castle-durham-to-open-after-restoration|title=Auckland Castle in Durham to open to public after £12.4m restoration|work=The Guardian|date=25 October 2019}}{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-tees-49663538|title=Auckland Castle to re-open after multimillion-pound restoration|publisher=BBC|date=11 September 2019}}{{cite web|url=https://www.aucklandproject.org/eat-and-shop/|title=Eat & shop|publisher=The Auckland Project|access-date=28 October 2019|archive-date=28 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728231408/https://www.aucklandproject.org/eat-and-shop/|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=https://www.aucklandproject.org/the-bishops-of-durham-through-time/|title=The Bishops of Durham Through Time|publisher=The Auckland Project|access-date=28 October 2019|archive-date=28 October 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191028142255/https://www.aucklandproject.org/the-bishops-of-durham-through-time/|url-status=dead}} Additional work continued at and near the castle to make the town a significant tourist attraction. Reports suggests that the revival of the area, dubbed the Auckland Project, will eventually cost a total of about £150m. === Binchester Roman Fort === {{Main|Binchester Roman Fort}} [[File:Binchester Roman Fort.jpg|thumb|[[Binchester Roman Fort]]|alt=The ruins of a building. The remains of stone walls up to about {{convert|1|ft|m|adj=on}} are all that remains.]] The route of the [[Roman road]] [[Dere Street]] passes straight through the middle of the town on its way to the nearby Roman Fort at [[Binchester]]. Binchester [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] Fort, or ''Vinovia'' as it was known to the Romans, has one of the best preserved examples of a Roman military [[Public bathing|bath house]] [[hypocaust]] in the country.{{Harvnb |Simpson|1991|pp=44–45}} Bishop Auckland's main shopping street, Newgate Street, together with Cockton Hill Road and Watling Road faithfully follow the route of Dere Street.{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=11}} Watling Road should not be confused with the Roman road [[Watling Street]], which is in the South of England. ==Transport== [[File:Bishop Auckland Railway Station.jpg|thumb|left|[[Bishop Auckland railway station]]|alt=In the foreground is a single storey building with a pitched roof. A railway platform runs along the length of the building. In the background is a large red warehouse style building.]] The town has links with the birth of the railways, with the original 1825 route of the [[Stockton and Darlington Railway]] passing through [[West Auckland, Durham|West Auckland]]. [[Timothy Hackworth]], a well-known locomotive builder, built steam locomotives in the neighbouring town of [[Shildon]].{{Cite ODNB | contribution = Hackworth, Timothy (1786–1850) | year = 2004 | title = Oxford Dictionary of National Biography | last = Carpenter | first = George W. | doi = 10.1093/ref:odnb/37500 | url = http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/37500 | access-date =26 January 2008 }} Today, [[Bishop Auckland railway station]] still provides passenger services, and is located at the end of the [[Tees Valley line]]. Since May 2010 it has been re-connected with the [[Weardale Railway]], which provides passenger services up the valley to [[Stanhope, County Durham|Stanhope]]. The town centre had a large railway goods yard until 1972. Freight traffic ceased to use the line completely in 1993 when [[Blue Circle]] cement stopped using the line to transport cement from its works in [[Eastgate, County Durham|Eastgate]].{{Harvnb |Hutchinson|2005|p=113}} The nearest airport to the town is [[Teesside Airport]] at around {{convert|19|mi|km}} drive South-East of Bishop Auckland. The nearest motorway junction is Junction 60 of the [[A1(M)]], which is around {{convert|8|mi|km}} away. The town has a bus station with a number of bus routes serving the town. Following the withdrawal of [[Go North East]] from the town on 8 April 2006, most of these services are provided by [[Arriva North East]].{{citation | title = Go-Ahead will use green diesel | work = [[The Northern Echo]] | date = 18 February 2006 | url = http://archive.thenorthernecho.co.uk/2006/2/18/218627.html | access-date =26 August 2008 }} However, a number of smaller firms such as Weardale Buses also serve the town. === Newton Cap viaduct === [[File:Newton Cap Viaduct (geograph 7488900).jpg|thumb|Newton Cap Viaduct]] The town also has a Grade II listed Victorian [[railway]] [[viaduct]] crossing the [[River Wear]].{{citation|title=Newton Cap Railway Viaduct|url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=1269762&resourceID=5|publisher=Heritage Gateway|access-date=21 September 2009}} At {{convert|105|ft|m}} high, the viaduct provides views of the surrounding countryside below as well as Auckland Castle, the Bishop's Park and the Town Hall on approaching the town from the Viaduct. It was originally built in 1857 to carry the Bishop Auckland to Durham City railway line across the River Wear and the Newton Cap Bank that leads down to the river. The railway closed in 1968 and the viaduct fell into a period of disuse and was at one point threatened with demolition.{{citation|title=Bridge leads to a rich vein of history|date=19 February 2002|url=http://archive.thenorthernecho.co.uk/2002/2/19/145400.html|work=[[The Northern Echo]]|access-date=8 August 2008}} However, in 1995, the viaduct was converted for vehicle use to take traffic on the [[A689 road|A689]] between Bishop Auckland and Crook, relieving the Grade I listed fourteenth-century single-lane Bishop [[Walter Skirlaw|Skirlaw]] bridge which sits in the valley below it.{{Harvnb|Hutchinson|2005|p=128}} On the north side of the bridge sits Eleven Arches Flatts Farm (named after the number of arches in the viaduct) which hosts [[Kynren]], a local historical '''Legend''' {{legend|#800080|[[Queen Elizabeth Sixth Form College]]}} {{legend|#000080|[[King James I Academy]]}} {{legend|#FF9900|[[St John's Catholic School]]}} {{legend|#FF0000|[[Bishop Auckland College]]}} {{legend|#000000|National average}} {{legend|#FF00FF|LEA average}}|alt=A chart illustrating the A-Level point scores discussed in the main text]] The town itself has three [[secondary school]]s—[[St John's Catholic School]], The [[Bishop Barrington Academy]] and [[King James I Academy]]. The town also has a college, [[Bishop Auckland College]] serving the [[Further Education]] and [[Higher Education]] fields. Both Bishop Barrington and King James schools have long histories, being founded in 1810 by [[Prince-Bishop|Bishop]] [[Shute Barrington|Barrington]] and in 1604 on the orders of [[James I of England|King James I]] respectively.{{citation | last = Lewis | first = Samuel | title = A Topographical Dictionary of England | publisher = S. Lewis & co | year = 1831 | pages = 108–112 | volume = 1 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=L88qAAAAMAAJ}}{{harvnb|Hutchinson|2005|pp=75–77}} In the government's Level 2 [[contextual value added|CVA]] (Contextual Value Added) statistic, which measures how much a school improves students between the end of [[National Curriculum for England|National Curriculum]] [[Key Stage 2]] and the end of [[Key Stage 4]], compared with how much other schools in the country improve students with similar circumstances, King James scored 1039.9 points, Barrington 1019.3 points and St John's scored a below average 997.4 points (with 1000 points being the target baseline). At [[A-Level]] in 2009, none of the towns sixth form centres average points scores reached the national average of 739.1 A-Level points per student or the LEA average of 664.1 points. Amongst sixth form centres in the town, St John's performed best with an average score of 661.5 points per student. In comparison, King James had an average A-Level score of 557 points and Bishop Auckland College with 459.3 points taking last position in the LEA in terms of A-Level point score, a position occupied by King James in the previous year. The Bishop Barrington Academy no longer has its own [[sixth form]], with the school being a feeder for [[Queen Elizabeth Sixth Form College]] in [[Darlington]]. The average A-Level points score at Queen Elizabeth is 871.8. The needs of those with [[Special education in the United Kingdom|special educational needs]] are served by Evergreen Primary. The town is served also by the following primary schools; Cockton Hill Infant, Cockton Hill Junior, Copeland Road Primary, Etherley Lane Primary, Oakley Cross Primary, St Andrew's Primary, St Anne's CofE Primary, St Helen Auckland Community Primary, St Wilfrid's RC Primary, Woodhouse Community Primary, Evergreen Primary School, Prince Bishops Community Primary School. Water supply comes from [[Burnhope Reservoir]] via the Wear Valley water treatment works at [[Wearhead]]. The present treatment works replaced old works on the site of the present one and another one closer to the town at [[Tunstall Reservoir]].{{citation | title = Royal visit to award-winning water treatment works | publisher = [[Northumbrian Water]] | date = 22 November 2005 | url = http://www.nwl.co.uk/newsreleases2005_3042.aspx | access-date = 21 February 2009 | archive-date = 16 May 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080516040227/http://www.nwl.co.uk/newsreleases2005_3042.aspx | url-status = dead }} Contrary to popular belief, the town does not receive water from [[Kielder Reservoir]]. Although water from Kielder can be pumped into the [[River Wear]], via the Tyne–Tees tunnel, upstream at [[Frosterley]], this water is not abstracted from the river until it reaches [[Chester-le-Street]]. Equally, although water can be pumped from the tunnel into [[Waskerley Reservoir]], which in turn supplies Tunstall Reservoir, Tunstall water treatment works was closed in 2004, when the new Wear Valley works was brought into service.{{citation |title = Water Resources Drought Plan |publisher = [[Northumbrian Water]] |date = April 2008 |url = http://www.nwl.co.uk/Final_published_drought_plan_April_2008.pdf |pages = 19–20 |access-date = 21 February 2009 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719052151/http://www.nwl.co.uk/Final_published_drought_plan_April_2008.pdf |archive-date = 19 July 2011}}{{citation | first = David | last = Archer | author2 = Chris Gibbins | title = Hydrological and species-specific responses to water transfers into the River Wear, northeast England. | journal = Proceedings of a Boulder Symposium July 1995 | publisher = [[International Association of Hydrological Sciences|IAHS]] | year = 1995 | url = http://www.cig.ensmp.fr/~iahs/redbooks/a230/iahs_230_0207.pdf | access-date = 6 June 2009 | pages = 207–218 }}{{dead link|date=July 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The electricity [[distribution network operator]] for the area is the [[CE Electric UK|CE Electric]]-owned [[Northern Electric|NEDL]] (Northern Electric Distribution Limited). Bishop Auckland ( AWK-lənd) is a market town and civil parish at the confluence of the River Wear and the River Gaunless in County Durham, England. It is 12 miles (19 km) northwest of Darlington and 12 miles (19 km) southwest of Durham.
Much of the town's early history surrounds the Bishops of Durham and the establishment of Auckland Castle's predecessor, a hunting lodge, which became the main residence of Durham Bishops. This is reflected in the first part of the town's name. During the Industrial Revolution, the town grew rapidly as coal mining became its largest industry. Decline in the coal mining industry during the late twentieth century has changed the town's largest sector to manufacturing.
Since 1 April 2009, the town's local authority has been Durham County Council. The unitary authority replaced the previous Wear Valley District and Durham County councils. The parliamentary constituency of Bishop Auckland is named after the town. It is currently held by Sam Rushworth of the Labour Party. The town is twinned with the French town of Ivry-sur-Seine.
